lesson.title: The Acid Test: Why Enzymes Need Their Chemical Comfort Zone
lesson.summary: Each enzyme has an optimal pH where its charged amino acid side chains hold the correct shape, and pH shifts away from that optimum weaken those charge based bonds and can denature the enzyme.
lesson.body:
Enzymes are proteins, and many of the amino acid side chains that stick out along a protein's folded structure carry an electrical charge, positive or negative, depending on how many hydrogen ions are attached to them. Because pH is a direct measure of hydrogen ion concentration, changing the pH of an enzyme's environment changes how many of those side chains are protonated, which changes their charge. Since ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds between charged and polar side chains help hold an enzyme's tertiary structure together, and often help position the substrate correctly inside the active site, shifting pH shifts the enzyme's shape and function.

Every enzyme has an optimal pH range where the charges on its key side chains are exactly right, both to maintain the correct overall folded shape and, in many cases, to directly participate in catalysis at the active site itself, since some reaction mechanisms require a side chain to donate or accept a proton at a precise step. Move the pH modestly away from that optimum and activity declines as those charge based interactions weaken. Move it far enough away and the ionic and hydrogen bonds holding the protein's structure together break down entirely, the enzyme denatures, and, much like extreme heat, the change is often permanent.

The stomach enzyme pepsin illustrates just how specifically an enzyme's optimum reflects its working environment: pepsin digests proteins in gastric fluid with a pH around one and a half to two, among the most acidic conditions found anywhere in the human body, and it would barely function, let alone survive, at a neutral pH. Trypsin, which continues protein digestion a short distance further along the digestive tract in the small intestine, has an optimal pH closer to eight, in the mildly basic range created there by bicarbonate secretions. Neither enzyme would work well in the other's environment, because each one's charged side chains are tuned to a different hydrogen ion concentration.

This pH sensitivity is not a flaw; it is a built in regulatory feature that the body exploits deliberately. Pepsin is synthesized as an inactive precursor, pepsinogen, that only becomes active once it meets stomach acid, and it is automatically shut off again once partially digested food moves into the neutral to basic environment of the small intestine, protecting the intestinal lining from an enzyme meant only for the stomach. The same physical sensitivity that makes pH dangerous to an enzyme in the wrong compartment makes it a convenient, self limiting switch when the compartments themselves differ in pH.

Temperature and pH act on enzymes through different physical routes, thermal motion breaking weak bonds in one case, altered ionic charge disrupting them in the other, but the underlying lesson is the same one first raised by the active site and induced fit model: an enzyme's function is inseparable from its precise three dimensional shape, and anything that reliably disturbs that shape, whether heat, acid, base, or an inhibitor at the active site, disturbs the enzyme's ability to do its job.
